page_title: 3 Kinds of Good Tech Debt — Squarespace Engineering Blog

summary.title: 3 Kinds of Good Tech Debt
summary.one_liner: Intentional tech debt, such as scaffolding, hardcoding, and leaving low-impact edge cases unfixed, can speed up delivery when its costs and limitations are understood and documented.
keywords: tech debt as financial debt analogy
takeaways: Tech debt can be an intentional investment: treat future work as a cost you choose to take on, like a mortgage.
Scaffolding: build the riskiest parts first and make a cheap, disposable version to get real-world feedback sooner, with stakeholders aware it will be replaced.
Hardcoding can beat a database-backed CMS when changes are infrequent and delays are acceptable; check limitations, whether Git is an acceptable update UI, and whether existing patterns exist.
Low-impact edge cases (like a race condition that allows one extra item) may be worth leaving unfixed if you verify they rarely occur and the impact is small.
Good tech debt is intentional, has clear documented limitations, and err on the side of building too little.
summary.summary: The author argues that tech debt, defined as future work, can be deliberately chosen rather than always accidental, and frames it with a financial-debt analogy. The post gives three case studies from Squarespace projects: building throwaway scaffolding for the email editor so it could get feedback early, hardcoding seasonal dashboard content in a YAML file edited through Git instead of building a CMS, and leaving a race condition in a 10-item limit unfixed after checking it did not occur in production. It closes with guidance to build little, make code easy to throw away, and document known limitations.
